title: The Watchmaker
summary:
William Paley began Natural Theology (1802) on a heath. If he kicked a stone, he wrote, he might answer that for all he knew it had lain there forever. But if he found a watch, its parts shaped and fitted together to tell the time, he would conclude it had a maker, even if he had never seen a watch made. Living things, like the eye, are fitted to their purposes far more intricately than any watch; so they too must have a designer.

David Hume had already pressed objections, in Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779): we have seen watches made, but never worlds; the world is as much like an animal or a plant as a machine; and the argument cannot tell one designer from many, or a skilled one from a bungler. Charles Darwin, who admired Paley, found a way for things to be fitted to purposes without anyone intending it: small variations, and natural selection, over immense time. Richard Dawkins called it The Blind Watchmaker (1986). The design argument lives on in new forms, such as the fine-tuning of the laws of physics.
